In mathematics, the '''Rankin–Cohen bracket''' of two [[modular form]]s is another modular form, generalizing the product of two modular forms.
{{harvs|txt|last=Rankin|authorlink=Robert Alexander Rankin|year=1956|year2=1957}} gave some general conditions for [[polynomial]]s in [[derivative]]s of modular forms to be modular forms, and {{harvs|txt|last=Cohen|authorlink=Henri Cohen (number theorist)|year=1975}} found the explicit examples of such polynomials that give Rankin–Cohen brackets. They were named by {{harvs|txt||last=Zagier|year=1994}}, who introduced Rankin–Cohen algebras as an abstract setting for Rankin–Cohen brackets.

==Definition==

If <math>f(\tau)</math> and <math>g(\tau)</math> are modular forms of weight ''k'' and ''h'' respectively then their ''n''th Rankin–Cohen bracket [''f'',''g'']<sub>''n''</sub> is given by 
:<math>[f,g]_n = \frac{1}{(2\pi i)^n}\sum_{r+s=n} (-1)^r\binom{k+n-1}{s}\binom{h+n-1}{r} \frac{\mathrm{d}^r f}{\mathrm{d}\tau^r}\frac{\mathrm{d}^s g}{\mathrm{d}\tau^s} \ . </math>
It is a modular form of weight&nbsp;''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''h''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''n''. Note that the factor of <math>(2\pi i)^n</math> is included so that the q-expansion coefficients of <math>[f, g]_n</math> are rational if those of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are. <math>\mathrm d^rf/\mathrm d\tau^r</math> and <math>\mathrm d^s g/\mathrm d\tau^s</math> are the standard [[derivative]]s, as opposed to the derivative with respect to the square of the [[Nome (mathematics)|nome]] which is sometimes also used.

==Representation theory==

The mysterious formula for the Rankin–Cohen bracket can be explained in terms of [[representation theory]]. Modular forms can be regarded as lowest weight vectors for [[discrete series representation]]s of SL<sub>2</sub>('''R''') in a [[function space|space of functions]] on SL<sub>2</sub>('''R''')/SL<sub>2</sub>('''Z'''). The [[tensor product]] of two lowest weight representations corresponding to modular forms ''f'' and ''g'' splits as a [[direct sum]] of lowest weight representations indexed by non-negative integers ''n'', and a short calculation shows that the corresponding lowest weight vectors are the Rankin–Cohen brackets [''f'',''g'']<sub>''n''</sub>.

==Rings of modular forms==
The first Rankin–Cohen bracket is the Lie bracket when considering a [[ring of modular forms]] as a [[Lie algebra]].
